This game has a gorgeous aesthetic and wonderful atmosphere. The team have done wonders to make a beautiful game with minimal jank (I did not encounter any bugs or poor performance in my playthrough) and a charming aesthetic despite limitations of scope and team. You don't feel rushed while playing and can easily explore whatever you like to your heart's content. The same applies for the choices as there's no rush or time limit to your decisions.

Far from being difficult, the puzzles/mysteries you solve to progress the plot are straightforward and pleasant, without either holding your hand too much or leaving you in the dark. Disco Elysium this is not, however, and you don't have much freedom to pursue sidequests or explore outside your main objective. But that is not the point of this game. You have a narrative, which the game sticks to faithfully without diluting its main ideas. 

The story and characters themselves is where things really shine. Quite a lot is made obvious as the plot goes along, though you are given hints to read between the lines and speculate on your own. There is plenty to enjoy whether you like overanalysing or simply going along with whatever the story asks of you, the revelations are satisfying even if you happen to predict them. 

Overall, a delightful game with a calming and nostalgic feel to it, and an engaging story to boot! <3

Résumé : je suis très satisfait par Herald et j'ai passé un très bon moment même si les deux premiers chapitres sont courts. Avec quelques corrections techniques, un bon développement de l'intrigue (plus de deux autres chapitres ?) et (peut-être) des ajouts aux chapitres existants Herald pourrait devenir un hit.

-------------

Points positifs

Très beau jeu empreint de réalisme quotidien mais où surgit l'inattendu. On peut vivre une aventure sans sauter à pied joint dans l'extravagance. Les graphismes, la bande sonore et les dialogues sont sublimes et leur enchaînement est si délicat qu'on se laisse captiver rapidement. C'est réjouissant de voir un tel niveau d'esthétique et de raffinement. Deux autres chapitres doivent suivre mais les chapitres existants pourraient en eux-mêmes être développés. La scène finale du deuxième chapitre semble ne pas permettre de prolonger les événements introductifs sur le bateau alors que la scène introductive du premier chapitre donne un sentiment tout contraire. J'attends avec impatience la suite.

J'ai apprécié pour une fois que l'histoire soit sérieuse (désolé, pas d'humour dans Herald) et réaliste (pas cyberpunk, d'enquête criminelle ou et de fin du monde, hein).

Les interactions avec l'environnement sont faciles et clairs.

Les PNJ inutiles à l'avancement de l'histoire pendant un sous-chapitre ne sont pas loquaces : une phrase aléatoire et pas de dialogue. Impossible de tenir une discussion avec eux. On peut trouver cela un peu court mais j'ai aimé ne pas avoir à faire avec des personnages secondaires aux dialogues baclés ou qui répètent comme des perroquets. C'était bien plus réalistes. Il y a possibilité d'ajouté des développements avec tous ces autres personnages à portée de main.

Des emplacements deviennent inaccessibles temporairement si l'intrigue implique de se focaliser sur une tâche. Mais il y a tout de même encore une liberté d'exploration dans les lieux accessibles. Encore une fois c'est une contrainte élégante et tellement réaliste ! On ne peut pas faire n'importe quoi n'importe quand dans ce jeu. Cela donne un cheminement efficace où on est rarement ou même pas du tout laissé dans le doute mais on peut satisfaire sa curiosité tout de même. Un équilibre proprement génial.

Le temps lui aussi est bien scandé : nuit, jour, lumière, repas, météo.

Pas de mauvais mélange de genre. Dans Herald il n'y a pas de puzzle.

Point négatifs

D'autres personnes ont soulignés les défaillances du système de sauvegarde. Après les avoir lu je n'ai pas éteint le jeu avant de l'avoir fini pour ne pas avoir de problème. Pour ma part je dirai je les deux premiers chapitres furent si court que je n'aurait pas eut besoin de sauvegarder et je ne peut pas dire si le système est défaillant. Il est vrai qu'à chaque transition scénaristique il serait agréable de voir un message indiquant d'une sauvegarde automatique a été effectuée et mentionner quelque part sur le menu d'accueil comment le jeu gère les sauvegardes pour que le joueur n'ai pas peur de perdre sa partie.

Les déplacements sont peu aisés. Quand l'icône des "pas" apparaît, cliquer ne déplace pas toujours le personnage. Dans ce type de jeu les scènes figées et les déplacements scénarisés sont plus fonctionnels à mon goût. Pour un moteur 3D je trouve tout de même que les déplacements contraints de Herald sont bien meilleurs que d'autres plus libres comme par exemple ceux de Syberia 3.

Il y a une contrepartie de la bonne gestion des contraintes des dialogues, des temps et des lieux. L'intrigue progresse très vite et on se retrouve un peu sur sa faim. Une traversée en mer c'est long habituellement. J'ai trouvé les deux premiers chapitres trop courts. Je vais les refaire avec d'autres choix mais je doute que cela donne plus de profondeur. Ce sera juste une alternative. Deux chapitres de plus semblent insuffisants.

This story takes place on a ship named The Herald, in an alternate historical timeline, during the mid-1800s. Perhaps they wanted to highlight how horrendous the British Empire was for all their means of colonization, but without directly naming Great Britain? Or perhaps it's a criticism of colonization all together, as the colonization of parts of Central America (or "New Spain") is mentioned as well. A large aspect of the story revolves around indigo trade, which was literally subsidized with slavery (of Native Americans and black people) and cheap labor (by Colonial India). Though the story doesn't name India directly, it is heavily implied that that's where the protagonist and the other main character are from. A newspaper clipping speaks of revolts in the colonies, which specifically did happen in Colonial India. Though it isn't mentioned in the story, in reality, the British government slaughtered countless people in India in order to suppress the uprising. Meanwhile, throughout the story, non-white characters deal with subtle or passive racism from their white colleagues. 

As the story is yet to be finished, I don't have full thoughts developed on the story as a whole, but I did enjoy this first half of it. It also has a really interesting plot twist. I like historical fiction, so I recommend it to anyone else that does as well.

That said, I agree with the other reviewers that worried from the first several minutes of the game whether you can bear to keep going.  No one wants to hear a lecture on history even if it provides the foundation for the events that follow.  The story is, in fact, very involving once the plot gets rolling, you bond with the cast  and suddenly, the 2nd half will be over.  The voice acting is excellent. [u]Review für Buch I + II[/u]

[i]Herald: An Interactive Period Drama[/i] ist, wie der Name schon vermuten lässt, ein Point & Click Abenteuer, welches in einem alternativen 19. Jahrhundert angesiedelt ist, in dem der Westen sich als koloniale Supermacht vereint hat. Wir spielen einen jungen Mann namens [i]Devan Rensburg[/i], der auf der Suche nach seinen Wurzeln ist. So verschlägt es ihn als Steward auf das Handelsschiff [i]HLV Herald[/i], welches auf den Weg in sein Geburtsland ist.

Ohne irgendwelche Superkräfte oder einer verrückten Fantasywelt, schafft es das niederländische Entwicklerstudio [i]Wispfire[/i], allein durch realistische Charaktere und einer ebenso glaubhaften Handlung, die auch aktuelle Gesellschaftsprobleme behandelt, den Spieler zu fesseln und auch zum nachdenken anzuregen. Alles jedoch ohne die Moralkeule zu schwingen.

Der Charakter unseres Protagonisten, [i]Devan Rensberg[/i], lässt sich durch die verschiedenen Antwort-, sowie Interaktionsmöglichkeiten sehr gut personalisieren, ohne dass er dabei aber seinen Kern verliert und alles perfekt ins Geschehen passt. Auch die Nebencharaktere sind sehr vielschichtig und wenn man die verschieden Dialogvaritaionen ausprobiert, merkt man schnell, dass man sie nicht so einfach in "gut" und "böse" einteilen kann, wie es bei anderen Spielen oft der Fall ist. Auch durch die unterschiedlichen Enden von Buch II und das Erreichen der 100% Errungenschaften, ist ein hoher Wiederspielwert gegeben. Ich habe in jedem Spieldurchgang noch etwas Neues entdeckt und so wurden die einfachen Aufgaben, denn Rätsel gibt es in diesem Spiel nicht, trotzdem nicht langweilig.

Neben den bereits genannten Punkten, besticht  [i]Herald: An Interactive Period Drama[/i] mit einer sehr liebevoll gestalteten 3D Grafik, einem wunderschönen und immer passenden Soundtrack, sowie 13 fantastischen Synchronsprechern, die den Charakteren Leben einhauchen und die Emotionen glaubhaft vermitteln. Ein Logbuch gibt einem außerdem noch weitere nützliche Informationen über das Schiff, die Charaktere, sowie der Spielewelt.

Einziger Kritikpunkt: Ich wünschte man könnte selber Speichern.

Ich bin auf jeden Fall gespannt auf Buch III & IV. Laut Entwicklerseite wurden die Gelder genehmigt und es werden zur Zeit 2D und 3D Künstler gesucht :)

Beklediğimden çok daha başarılı bir macera oyunu. Aslında tam olarak macera denemez, çünkü envanter namına pek bir şeyimiz yok ama gerek anlattığı hikâye gerekse de karakterleriyle sizi kendine bağlamayı başarıyor.

Bir ticaret gemisine tayfa olarak yazılan, Devan adındaki bir genci yönetiyoruz oyunda. Doğal olarak ilk işimiz kaptanın gözüne girmeye çalışmak ve diğer tayfalarla kaynaşmak. İşin güzel tarafı oyunda ilerledikçe kendinizi gerçekten de mürettebatın bir parçası gibi hissetmeye ve karakterleri gerçekten de önemsemeye başlamanız. Hepsinin kendince bir yaşam hikâyesi ve hayat görüşü var. 

Yolculuk sırasında pek çok aksilik yaşanıyor doğal olarak. Biz de bunları dostlarımızın başı belaya girmeden, barışçıl yollarla çözmeye çalışıyoruz. Ama istersek tam tersini yapıp kurallara sıkı sıkıya bağlı kalmak ve hepsinin kaptan tarafından cezalandırılmasını sağlamak da elimizde. Hatta birkaç yerde başarısız olabiliyor, birilerinin ölümüne bile sebep olabiliyoruz. 

Hepsinin üstüne hikaye içinde hikaye tekniği uyguluyor oyun. Gemide yaptıklarımız aslında daha önce yaşanmış olaylardan oluşuyor ve Devan tüm bu süre zarfında bunları kendisini esir tutan, gizemli bir kadına anlatıyor. Bölüm başlarında ve sonlarında esir tutulduğumuz bu yerde de ufak bölümler oynuyoruz. Oyunun seslendirmeleri, grafikleri ve müzikleri de bir o kadar başarılı.

Ne yazık ki stüdyo maddi krize girmiş ve oyunun son iki bölümünü yapmakta zorlanıyorlar. Eğer imkânınız varsa indirime girmesini beklemeden satın alıp destek olabilirsiniz. Zaten sadece 18 lira. Bunu cidden hak ediyorlar.

Herald is a gripping tale with good pacing with unraveling mysteries as you are aboard the ship "Herald". Your choices feel weighted and like it matters. I didn't know what to expect story-wise, but the game really exceeded my expectations in both script and voice acting. The characters feel genuine and they are unique in their own ways that it makes you feel like you are really a part of the story. You can be a defiant or an obedient steward, and how characters and the story unravels depend on that. I was beyond surprised when I learned that the team behind this game consists of only 4 people. 

Of course, I will be fair and mention a few cons to the game. Although the art is very stylistic, the graphics can be polished more and some movements feel slow and sluggish, especially when inspecting items. I love interactive stories, and Herald being a choice-driven narrative was why I took an interest in it in the first place.

I thought quite a few of the 3D models seemed to have rather big heads in proportion to their bodies, but after a while I realised it is a rather endearing trait. The voice acting was great, but perhaps because I've just played Masquerada, I find that the voice acting here wasn't as good in comparison. (However, it was definitely not badly done; Masquerada's VA set a really high standard.)

I did not realise this was a Point and Click game when I bought this. Somehow I had missed that. That being said, I didn't mind clicking around and discovering things during my first playthrough. Though, the Encyclopedia was a bit clunky to navigate and the size of the text didn't lend well to reading all the information, so I did skip over quite a bit.

The beginning of the story was rather confusing especially without much context. Especially after being told that my choices would affect the story, I was intially wary since it seemed like no matter what I chose was wrong somehow. However, the story does pick up once we get on board the HLV Herald. After that, I didn't want to stop until I got to the end.

Since only Books I & II have been released, it is hard to say how good or tight the entire plot is. However, from what I've seen so far, I don't think I'll be disappointed. From my 3 playthroughs to get all the achievements, it's already interesting to see the variations in the storyline.

I enjoyed reading the letters in the Archives as well. They provided additional information on the characters. The handwriting fonts, though pretty, were almost impossible to read, especially on my small laptop screen. Zooming in was also a pain, and I ended up reading the plain text for all of them.

Although short, it's a solid game if you like choice-driven adventures.

A super refreshing throwback to the days of point-and-click adventure games with an even more refreshing modern way of storytelling. This game, featured in an alternate 19th century universe, brings up topics such as politics, race, and gender in a way a lot of mainstream games struggle to. The characters are likable and the end of each Book holds a massive twist that leaves you definitely wanting more. 

The developers have posted that Books 3 & 4 will be delayed due to funding, but nevertheless all the more reason to try out their demo then decide to buy the game, Wispfire is a new development team that has absolutely grasped me into looking forward into whatever stories they want to tell next.

A charming visual novel with a dash of point&click, though don't let this game's(beautiful) visual mislead you, since it soon finds it's roots in the mystery genre and could deceive when it dedicates its narrative to some heavy topics. Addressing all those it wishes to address with the necessary weight, without bashing it over your head with an anvil. 

The narrative follows the "how-we-got-here" model, recounting the sea voyage of a man trying to reconnect with his roots. He finds himself instead being dragged into the mysteries surrounding his fellow passangers on the titular ship, while framing it in the form of a flashback that Devan himself is narrating. 
The story takes place in a semi-alternative history and apparently with a lot of research dedicated to it, even if the game itself uses it mostly for worldbuilding and character backgrounds. [i] Show, don't tell [/i] works well here together with the documents and books you can find and read to fill in the blanks. After all, the story takes place on a relatively medium staffed ship (for now), so with a smaller cast of characters and flows well with it's plots and twists, actually delivering some solid emotional punches and motivating to play on. Like reading a good book. 

It was nice to see some more thoughtless answers have matching consequences and affecting relationships a little, though you shouldn't expect heavy branching. This game has a story to tell and it follows that. The gameplay mechanics themselves may seem a bit stiff and outdated, but it's the narrative and worldbuilding that is more the focus here.

Out of my own preferences I also must really point out the superb voice acting for basically every character and nice sound design(effects+ Soundtrack). And characters of course. In a genre like this you need to have someone to root for. Which works in Herald's favor, because most of cast have their own little secrets or are at least intriguing, if not yet fully utilized at this point (currently II chapters released out of IV) and it's obvious that the story is just now growing out of it's build-up stage.
And I really wish to know the how-we-got-here.

Herald's subtitle describes itself succinctly: it's a narrative-driven point-and-click adventure set in an alternate version of the 19th century. Something befell the HLV Herald, and our protagonist Devan Rensburg recounts and relives the events leading up to the apparent tragedy. Maneuvering through the ship isn't always the smoothest experience, but that hardly matters—the real draw is conversing with the Herald's motley cast. Each story-relevant character is wonderfully written and voice acted, with beautiful portrait art to match. Everyone has their own motivations and goals; while the story has a fixed structure, you can make choices to alter the tone of discussions and decide who you can trust... or betray their trust in you.

The story is fairly short and unfortunately half-finished, but I'm eagerly anticipating the conclusion of this tale, whenever it can be completed.

The game takes place in an alternate history where 1800's Europe and its colonies are unified under a single republican government, the Protectorate.  

You play Devan, a young man in search of identity and adventure as you set out to sea towards the lands of the east where you born, but never got to experience.  Along the way, you'll make choices that affect events not unlike recent Telltale games.  Be prepared to encounter some weighty topics like colonialism, racism, feminism, and classism.

As only Books I and II are released as of this review, be prepared for a very short game with a "to be continued" ending.  Books III and IV will be released at some point in the future to conclude the story.

Overall, worth the $10 I paid and I'm looking forward to the final two episodes.

[h1]Herald is a tightly woven dramatic interactive novel, which plays like a mystery play. Some beauty knows no language. But, this beautifully animated point & click choice based drama crosses language and race barriers with issues that we struggle with today like suicide, faith, racism, gun control, interpersonal relationships, & slavery; all set in the 19th Century.[/h1]

It seems that, in Herald, I am everyman and every woman. The script draws us in to experience the motives & thoughts of each character. The narrative, characterizations, art, & voice acting are incredibly well done. 

[b]Gameplay Mechanics:[/b]
The game plays out via simple p&c mechanics, where you use a mouse click to move through the ship. Controller options have recently been patched in, and are still being tweaked. The narrative is revealed in textboxes, where in parts it is just dialogue advanced by clicks, interspersed with sets of choices. Dialog is followed by cutscenes that are enjoyable and advance the story. I never got bored even after multiple games. The save system is convenient, making it possible to reload the chapter if you feel you made bad choices.

[b]Graphics & Sound:[/b]
The soundtrack is lovely! One particularly haunting tune that appears in the theme is played on the piano by a character in one scene, who sings the words. This means a soundtrack would definitely be a plus.
Even with a good machine, the framerate never went above 30 fps for me. I felt like this was intentional, as it creates a not quite slow-mo effect, lending a dramatic flair to each scene. If lower framerates bother you, this may not be the game for you. 
Most of the animations were done well, if simply. Most character movements seem true. There is one point where a character walks through a door, and then the irritating movements of the doctor helping a patient. Almost comical, the doc’s eyebrow moves side to side in one conversation.  But, in most other scenes, it is almost entrancing to see that simple can be elegant.

[b]Where Herald Succeeds & Fails with Choices:[/b]  

[u]Mystery/ Foreshadowing[/u] Herald is a mystery in its whole. At this point, only the 1st 2 books are released, so there is much to work with here and the writers seem to have taken full advantage of that, succeeding in every account. 
✔  There is a revealer in the final scene of the 2nd book that changes what you thought you knew in very early scenes. This leaves you with a cliff hanger of sorts. 
✔  Even multiple play-throughs add to and expand your opinions of different characters. Some things are never answered for us, but we are left to form our own opinions. 
 ✔  Some apparent mysteries are left open at the end, hinted at only by shadows and shapes in the artwork. 
✔  Ultimately, characters are left to being human with various interpretations of their behavior still being available after several replays.

[u]Complexity of Choice[/u] 
I rate the choice in Herald a solid 8 out of 10. I played Choice of Robots, an excellent choice game that was totally text-based. I would rate that as a perfect 10, because your choices changed everything. The choice web was intricate, creating literally hundreds of outcomes. But, games like Firewatch, which I also loved but would rate a 5, presented only cosmetic changes with the choices. The players were all drawn back into the original plot line at collection points, so that ultimately your choices did not really change the story in Firewatch. 
✔  In Herald, there is one story. The narrative rules as a mystery which you will reveal over the course of not only these current 2 books, but future books. But, your choices can affect the interplay of characters, and the outcome of scenes, and the appearance of different dialog trains. Information which you have not revealed is not later available in a conversation. 
✘  Many decisions often affect only that immediate tier, and sometimes only in the emotional feel of the dialog. For example, whether you offer to do Ian's job for him or not, you get to do it. Regardless of how you respond to the Rani in the prologue, the results are the same. And, with the captain, navigator, & senator, I was accused of taking so long whether I stalled or took the direct text options.
✔  Numerous choices can change whether a character lives, dies, or is in the brig. Some characters can appear earlier in a scene, or in the place of another character, if your responses change. Interestingly, if you choose to start at the scripted start of the 2nd book, instead of in the 1st, I discovered that the script goes with the option of no characters being dead.
✘  No choice seems to have an effect beyond its immediate scene, with the exception of whether certain players exist or not. Because of this & the save system, it is possible to exit to the menu and restart a book multiple times, to get multiple achievies at once. Basically, some crucial decisions will pop one of 3 different achievements. No achievement requires more than one scene’s set of responses to resolve, with the possible exception of Mad Discourtesy, which requires probably 2 scene’s answers.

[u]Replayability[/u]
✔  Despite the save/ reload ability, multiple playthroughs will probably be needed to get all achievements. Also, you won’t get all info in the mystery without at least 3 plays. My 1st play took about 8 hours, with reading everything, even the letters that are unlocked at the end and the credits. The 2nd play took 4 hours, still reading choices and popping some achievements. After that, additional plays took about a half hour per book with skipping dialog & quick choices. So, after experiencing everything the story has to offer thus far… in every nuance, I have almost 16 hours. 

[u]Dev Support[/u]
✔  The dev team has made the art available in the trading card collectables.
✔   A large collection of concept art was made available free in earlier release notes. They don’t seem to be attempting to monetize every bit of data, as many devs are doing. 
✔  They are responding quickly to comments and or email. 

[b]Suggestions for Improvement:[/b]
1. The log is helpful in-game, but access to what you’ve accumulated after the game would be a great addition to the menu. 
2. Voice acting could be added for the letter collections in the menu. (Only half of them seem to pop after these first two books.)
3. Having musical options & even a musical library in the menu, as with the letter archive, would be even better. Alternately, a soundtrack would be a plus.

[h1]With a storyline as deep as the ocean, & several currents relevant to any age, Herald is so much more than a lovely journey between the sea & the stars. As a choice-based p& c adventure game, Herald provides hours of mystery drama for fans of gaming narrative. I highly recommend the game, and I look forward to the exciting upcoming books.[/h1]

I really love this game, so much so that the moment I finished one playthrough, I started the next. The genius of Herald is the way it blends everything that's almost comfortingly familiar about adventure games and comes up with something entirely fresh and exciting. Many of the character archetypes (stern statesman, whiny cabin boy, underappreciated officer) are immediately familiar, but as the story unfolds every single character is given depth. The plot surprised me at multiple times (especially the end of Book II, loved it!), but it never felt forced because there were always clues laying the groundwork for every reveal. It seems you are bound to go through the same basic plot, but your choices certainly matter in some significant ways, some choices opening up or closing options later. And both books so far end with high stakes conversations with dramatic effects. I was surprised after I finished playing to enjoy reading the archives (letter and document style backstory pieces), which add further depth to several characters and help to explain their motivations. This is a rich story with lots of detail accessible to flesh it out, but even if you skip clicking around the ship for extra information, there's a lot to enjoy.

The changing of expressions and general movement of the portraits during conversation helps to give the already good voice acting a visual component to play off of. For a game like this where the soul is in the dialogue and choices, I think this works very well. 

I definitely recommend this game! Be aware that it deals with a variety of issues and topics of colonialism from several angles, so if you are sensitive to some content (violence, slavery mentions, racism) you may want to check for warnings to prepare yourself. That said it's a very well crafted story and I am eagerly looking forward to the rest of it!
